entries.title: AIPAC halts endorsements and direct contributions to candidates
entries.summary: The pro-Israel lobbying group and influential political funder announced it would no longer endorse candidates or give directly to campaigns. AIPAC's affiliated super PAC, though, will continue.
entries.content:
AIPAC halts endorsements and direct contributions to candidates

The pro-Israel political organization AIPAC, or the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, announced on Wednesday that it will no longer issue endorsements, make direct PAC contributions or earmark funds for candidates.

A longtime influential lobbying group, AIPAC started its direct political involvement five years ago. Since then, particularly this midterm election cycle, AIPAC has been met with mounting resistance. The group has faced criticism over its stances on various issues, including the wars in Gaza and Iran.

Candidates endorsed by AIPAC have also faced tough opposition from both the political right and the political left for accepting the organization's support and financial contributions as public opinion on the U.S. relationship with Israel has shifted. In order to tame the criticism, some AIPAC-endorsed candidates said they won't accept any money from the organization.

AIPAC first announced the changes in a letter to members, stating "the challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead." In the letter, AIPAC said it wouldn't stop funneling money to candidates that align with the group's mission by mobilizing individual donors.

"We will prioritize increasing direct, organized contributions from individual Americans to candidates—expanding upon our current efforts—and maximizing the emerging political fundraising tools," the letter said.

The letter added that the 2028 cycle will "demand an even stronger commitment by our activists to pro-Israel politics." As a result, the group plans to increase support "for the Republicans and Democrats who are advancing policies that strengthen America's alliance with Israel and standing up against anti-Israel legislation."

In a statement to NPR, AIPAC spokesperson Deryn Sousa said the group's mission and strategy remains the same despite the changes.

"Our goal is to build support for the U.S.-Israel relationship. AIPAC members gave more than $90 million directly to candidates this cycle, and that organized, direct giving from our members will continue and increase."

AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to candidates and political committees in 2026 through Sept. 30, according to FEC filings. Its affiliated super PAC United Democracy Project contributed $13 million to candidates and political committees and spent an additional $53.5 million in independent expenditures.

AIPAC confirmed with NPR that its affiliated super PAC, United Democracy Project, will continue to operate and will be able to raise an unlimited amount of money. It has spent heavily to support pro-Israel candidates, and oppose those who criticize Israel.

In recent days, several of the super PAC's individual independent expenditures are being used to campaign against Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan.

AIPAC also spent heavily to campaign against El-Sayed in the primary, backing his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. The Michigan Senate contest is just one of the high-profile races where AIPAC has spent in favor of a pro-Israel politician or in opposition to someone the organization sees as less favorable to Israel.

entries.title: The Justice Department begins notifying counties where it wants to monitor elections
entries.summary: The department has long deployed election monitors, but the Trump administration's unprecedented steps to try to wrestle control over elections have led to new concerns about DOJ monitoring this year.
entries.content:
The Justice Department begins notifying counties where it wants to monitor elections

The Department of Justice this week began notifying the counties it wants to monitor on Election Day, NPR has learned.

Counties in Colorado, Florida, Minnesota, Texas and Washington have received notifications from the Justice Department so far, but the list seems to be growing in real time.

The department has long deployed monitors to ensure compliance with voting laws, but the Trump administration's unprecedented steps to try to wrestle control over elections from local and state governments have led to new concerns about DOJ monitoring this year. And already this week, at least one county official is raising questions about why his locality is on the DOJ's list.

Last month, Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, said the department planned to send 1,000 observers nationwide, in what she termed "the largest monitoring effort" in DOJ history.

And even as counties are being notified, it's unclear which jurisdictions or how many the department plans to monitor this November. A DOJ spokesperson, Kiersten Pels, told NPR those details will be shared "closer to the election."

The Justice Department routinely observes elections. The department under President Biden monitored 64 jurisdictions in 24 states on Election Day in the last midterm year, 2022.

But to many local officials and experts, this year is different.

President Trump continues to falsely maintain that he won the 2020 election and that election fraud is more widespread than it has ever been proven to be. Experts worry federal law enforcement could potentially use those false claims — or others generated this year — as pretext to try to seize ballots during the counting period, or interfere in the process in some other way.

Most states reported no incidents with Justice Department monitors during primary elections earlier this year, but in Wyoming, the state's Republican governor expressed concern about "aggressive" and "irregular" behavior by monitors for the state's August primary. And the Republican county clerk of Laramie County told NBC News that the conduct of the monitors "showed complete disregard for our state laws and administration of our elections."

The Department of Justice disputes that characterization.

"We disagree with the public framing that the two monitors we sent were 'aggressive' or did anything improper," Pels said, adding that Dhillon had a meeting with the Wyoming officials after the fact.

In previous election cycles, state officials in the states where monitors were assigned were notified at the same time as the counties. This year, that did not happen initially, according to officials in three states who spoke to NPR anonymously because they weren't authorized to speak to the press. So states have been scrambling since the notifications began going out Tuesday to figure out where the DOJ plans to be.

After NPR asked the DOJ why states had not been notified, multiple state officials told NPR they then received notification from the department.

One of the counties that received a notification is Adams County, Colo.

The clerk there, Democrat Josh Zygielbaum, told NPR he wasn't shocked the DOJ selected his county to observe, as Adams County includes part of the state's 8th Congressional District, a toss-up district that could determine party control of the House of Representatives next year.

Zygielbaum was surprised however that the DOJ reached out only to him, and not the Republican clerk in neighboring Weld County, which also houses a sizable portion of that same congressional district.

"My initial thought is that it's politically motivated, and that this is potentially an intimidation technique," Zygielbaum said. "Although I like to assume the best in people, the administration really has shown its disdain for elections, particularly in states and counties where mail ballots exist."

Pels, of the DOJ, said the department prioritizes places with competitive elections, and would monitor Adams County because it is covered by Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act, which requires voters be given access to election materials in the language they speak. Weld County is not covered under that provision.

That explanation didn't fully comfort Zygielbaum.

"The fact that we're covered by Section 203 means we have a higher portion of Spanish-speaking voters who have a right to vote," Zygielbaum said. "It still doesn't put me at ease that it's not a targeted visit."

NPR reported in September that Trump administration officials assigned to noncitizen voting issues last year circulated a list of counties covered by Section 203, along with a DOJ criminal checklist outlining requirements for prosecution of voter-related charges.

Colorado state officials say they are considering how to respond to the DOJ's request, considering Colorado election rules say observers need to have permission from the secretary of state's office, unless they are ordered to observe by a court.

"We are considering these requests in collaboration with the Attorney General's Office," said Jack Todd, a spokesperson for the Colorado secretary of state's office.

Zygielbaum says his election processes won't change either way. He has, however, already requested a staffer from the state come to Adams County on Election Day just to keep an eye on the federal monitors if they do come.

"I have lots of questions about why they're there and what their ultimate intent is," he said.

NPR has confirmed the DOJ has also sent monitor notifications to seven counties in Texas, King County, Wash., Miami-Dade County, Fla., and Hennepin and Ramsey counties in Minnesota.

The DOJ requested to send monitors to the same Minnesota counties during the state's primary in August, but monitors were denied close access to polling locations. A spokesperson for the Minnesota secretary of state's office said it was too soon to know whether a different decision would be made for this fall's general election.

In 2024, Texas similarly blocked the Biden-era DOJ from election monitoring. Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and current Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, went to court then to block monitors from getting inside polling and counting locations.

"The DOJ knows it has no authority to monitor Texas elections and backed down when Texas stood up for the rule of law," Paxton said in a statement on Nov. 5, 2024.

entries.title: Poll: Voters want Congress to be a check on Trump, trust Democrats more on issues
entries.summary: A new poll shows record support for Democratic congressional candidates ahead of the midterms, as voters feel the party is better attuned to handling their top issues.
entries.content:
Poll: Voters want Congress to be a check on Trump, trust Democrats more on issues

Voters have record low trust in Republicans' ability to handle their top issues like immigration and rising prices, according to the latest Strength In Numbers/Verasight poll shared with NPR.

The poll also finds a strong majority of voters want the next Congress to undo President Trump's agenda — or act as a check on his power — on policies like tariffs and trade, health care and immigration.

Less than two weeks out from Election Day, voters say they'd prefer to elect a Democrat to Congress over a Republican by a double-digit margin among registered voters (52% to 41%) and likely voters (54% to 42%).

The survey of 2,028 respondents was conducted Oct. 13-19 and has a margin of sampling error of 2.2 percentage points, meaning results could be about 2.2 points higher or lower.

Trump's job approval sits at near-record lows for his second term, with just 34% approving of his performance and 62% disapproving, with 50% strongly disapproving.

G. Elliott Morris, author of the Strength In Numbers newsletter and CEO of polling company Wave Polling and Research, said the latest poll explains the current challenges with the political landscape Republicans face.

"Trump's ratings hit new lows on seven of the 10 issues we've tracked since May 2025, from jobs and trade to immigration and border security, and he's now underwater on every issue we ask about," Morris said. "The president's policies have even harmed Republicans, with voters now more likely to say they trust Democrats to handle the issues of immigration and the economy."

Among adults, prices and inflation are collectively mentioned far and away as the most important problem facing the country today, with 63% of respondents saying it was one of their top three most important problems and 39% listing it first. Other top issues include jobs and the economy, health care, elections and democracy and immigration.

Taken all together, the sentiment of the electorate explains why Democrats and Republicans are spending big in House and Senate races stretching deep into conservative territory where Trump performed well in 2024.

Loading...

Americans have soured on Trump and Republicans

Voters chose to give Republicans control of the White House and Congress in the 2024 election, and at least some of them say they regret their choice. According to the poll, nearly one in 10 people who said they voted in the 2024 presidential race regret their choice, including almost 15% of self-described Trump voters and 15% who backed a third-party candidate.

In May 2025, the Strength in Numbers/Verasight poll found voters trusted Republicans more than Democrats on immigration and deportations by an average of 15 points. Now, they trust Democrats by a narrow one point margin.

In every measure that the poll has tracked, Republicans have lost ground in the last year and a half, and only hold a slim advantage on crime and public safety issues and border security.

When asked which party voters trust to handle their personal top issue, Democrats hold a 47-35 advantage, a nearly 10-point jump since May 2025 and the widest gap measured.

Loading...

The midterms are a referendum

Many polls, including the September NPR/PBS News/Marist survey, find that the 2026 midterm choices are best viewed in relation to Trump rather than a pure binary vote of support for the Democratic or Republican candidates.

Only 25% of respondents said it was more important to elect a Congress that will help Trump pass his agenda, compared to 58% who said it was about electing a Congress to act as a check and balance on Trump.

Two of every five voters surveyed said their decision would mostly be a statement against Trump and his agenda, compared to one in five who said it would be a statement of support. For 20% of voters surveyed, their choice would be about specific issues and candidates in their district.

On the issues of tariffs and trade, health care, foreign policy, elections and voting, government spending and social programs, immigration and deportations and artificial intelligence, a majority of those surveyed want a Congress to roll back or act as a check on Trump's stances.

More voters think the Democratic Party cares more about people like them than Republicans, and 20% say neither party does.

entries.title: Meet the people moving north to escape increasingly hot summers
entries.summary: As climate change fuels hotter summers, some Britons are moving north in search of cooler weather. Could a similar shift be on the horizon in the United States?
entries.content:
Meet the people moving north to escape increasingly hot summers

LONDON – Mike Coe never thought he would leave his dream home in rural Worcestershire, not far from Stratford-upon-Avon, Shakespeare's birthplace.

That was until Coe started researching the warming temperatures in the region. Coe had a job making videos for environmental activists, and ten years ago, when he spoke to his colleagues about the effects of climate change – and read the scientific papers himself – he started to get concerned.

"I realized that it was likely to get very, very hot in the British Midlands, even during my lifetime," Coe, 69, told NPR. "I said… I think we need to move to Scotland." A decade later, now Coe and his partner Lizzie Stoodley live on the Isle of Skye off Scotland's west coast.

There they have built a "Passivhaus" — a highly energy-efficient home — the second they have built. And they are glad they built their new home where they did. "Our decision to move seems to have been confirmed as being the right one, particularly this year," Coe told NPR.

Friends who still live further south have told the couple that the weather was "unbelievably hot" and "incredibly uncomfortable" this summer, as the United Kingdom experienced its hottest summer on record, with five successive heat waves and widespread drought.

But while southern regions warmed up, the weather on the Isle of Skye remained temperate. "I think there are quite a few more very hot summers I might escape by living here rather than remaining where we did," Coe said.

Others are considering the same move.

Susan Chinnery and her partner Steve Lewis, used to live near Milton Keynes, 50 miles north of London. But they began finding the summer months increasingly uncomfortable.

"I hate the hot weather," Chinnery told NPR. "I remember 2022 when Steve and I… we were actually sleeping outside on the patio because it was just too hot to sleep indoors." Like many British homes, their Victorian-era house was designed to keep in the warmth, and doesn't have air conditioning.

Lewis said that 2022 reminded him of the famously hot British summer of 1976, and he realised it was only going to get warmer. "I thought to myself, it's arrived," he told NPR. "This is the slow and inexorable decline into some new state."

Last year, Chinnery and Lewis moved to Westray, one of the Orkney Islands off northern Scotland, largely because of rising temperatures.

Melissa Terras also moved to Scotland, partly because of climate change. "When I mentioned climate change to people as one of the reasons why we were going to move north, people laughed," Terras told NPR. "They were like, 'What are you talking about?'"

In 2017, Terras moved her family from Letchworth Garden City, a town 40 miles north of London, to Edinburgh. A professor at the University of Edinburgh, Terras chose a house "up a hill," mindful of rising sea levels. She says more people are now thinking as she did several years ago.

The trend is also emerging in the housing market. Real estate agents in the Scottish Highlands told NPR that more buyers are citing cooler summers as a factor in their home-buying decisions. Recent figures show that house prices in Scotland rose year over year, while they fell in southeastern England and Greater London.

All over Europe, there are signs that climate is beginning to influence where many people are choosing to live, alongside factors including jobs, housing and the economy.

Scientists say Europe is the world's fastest warming continent. Large areas of Europe saw scorching temperatures this summer, with widespread wildfires, and at least 35,000 excess deaths thought to have been linked to the heat.

As climate change intensifies, countries around the world are grappling with more extreme impacts. At this year's U.N. General Assembly, Nepal's prime minister, Balendra Shah, called recent flash floods in his country "a warning to the world," urging a "culture of preparedness" for future climate crises.

Gaia Vince, a London-based journalist and author of Nomad Century, predicts climate change will drive hundreds of millions of people from hotter regions to more temperate areas this century.

The U.K. has felt the effects, too. "We've had five almost consecutive heat waves this year alone, and our infrastructure is built for a completely different climate — everything is built for a climate which no longer exists," Vince told NPR.

Britain will also see migration, Vince said, as people adapt their lifestyles and infrastructure. Wealthier individuals are already moving toward places such as Ireland and Scotland in search of a more livable climate, she said.

Vince expects a similar trend in the United States, with the Great Lakes region and Alaska potentially attracting people from farther south.

Some Americans are already making the move to Scotland. Jason Sorensen, a California native, moved with his wife, Christine, last year to Golspie in the Scottish Highlands.

After experiencing wildfires in Los Angeles and hot summers while working in London, Sorensen said "something broke" inside him, and he decided he wanted to live somewhere cooler.

"Between now and 2100, there really are only a few places that you could categorize as 'best of the worst' oases if things really go to hell," Sorensen told NPR. "Certain parts of Norway, the South Island of New Zealand, maybe southern Chile down near the Lake District, maybe certain parts of Alaska — and northern Scotland."

Not so long ago, people who said they wanted to live in Scotland for the weather would have been laughed at.

But for many living farther south, it seems the joke isn't quite so funny anymore.

entries.title: Top 2 Democrats on Intel say they're preparing for Trump to claim foreign meddling
entries.summary: The top Democrats on the House and Senate intelligence committees said they are working under the presumption that the president will seek to justify election interference by alleging fraud.
entries.content:
Top 2 Democrats on Intel say they're preparing for Trump to claim foreign meddling

The top Democrats on the House and Senate intelligence committees say they are operating under the presumption that President Trump and his allies will allege fraud related to this year's midterms in order to justify election interference.

"We start with the premise that the president is going to do that. It would be irresponsible not to, speaking as somebody who was in the chamber on January 6, 2021," said Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn. "We're making the assumption that the president is not going to accept the results of what looks to be a very challenging election for him and his party."

Speaking alongside Himes on Wednesday, Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said that one way the president could do that: claiming foreign interference in the voting process.

"President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis in a statement to NPR. "While extreme Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump Administration is taking decisive action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion."

Asked if he would accept the results of the election by a reporter earlier this month, Trump replied, "What do you think? Of course I will, but we don't want cheating."

Himes and Warner are members of the Gang of Eight, senior lawmakers who oversee the nation's spy agencies and receive confidential briefings.

In a briefing for reporters, Warner and Himes said they have made clear to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and other intelligence leaders that they must be immediately reachable by phone on and after Election Day in the event that Trump alleges foreign interference in the election. Or, Himes said, if the president "decides to use allegations of foreign interference as an excuse to seize ballot boxes, question the validity of the election."

"If, at noon on Election Day, the president announced that the Iranians have undertaken operation," Himes said, "I'm on TV saying 'I'm Gang of Eight and I have received no such briefing, no such information, and I have no reason to believe that this is accurate.'"

"Now, does that end the crisis? No, but that's the first step," Himes said.

Both lawmakers said that they are in close contact with top Trump intelligence officials, even as they allege that those leaders have failed to provide legally mandated pre-election reports to Congress assessing the state of play regarding foreign election meddling efforts.

"When Jay Clayton assumed his role as DNI, we asked and received the required classified summary of influence and interference," Himes said. "We have not received a bunch of things that we have asked for," including, he said the statutorily required reports about the state of play 120 days, 60 days and 30 days before the election.

The ODNI office did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

The lawmakers said that they had received one classified report on Tuesday from the DNI's office, which detailed what they described as a "grabbag" of intelligence on meddling efforts, including the sort of Russian and Chinese campaigns that have come to be expected in American elections.

"The state of play, I would argue, is Russia, similar to prior occasions, is going after Democrats, usually with misinformation," Warner said. "Iran is probably more looking at disruption in Europe. They've been more anti-Trump. China's been more selective, oftentimes on local races or smaller issues, oftentimes with Chinese nationals involved."

Still, Himes said that there is a "profound distinction" between those influence campaigns and actual interference in election infrastructure itself, "which is messing around with the voting rolls, with the machines … which is very, very difficult."

Himes specifically emphasized that "we have never seen an operation to actually interfere and, as of now, we are not seeing either the capability or the intent to interfere."

Their preparations for a possible fraudulent claim of foreign interference is one part of a much larger election integrity effort by the Democrats and good governance groups.

"There is a plan there," Warner said, noting that a constellation of more than 75 groups are still meeting on a regular basis, "fully lawyered up." But he suggested that the responsibility to protect democracy is much broader than good governance groups and lawmakers themselves, and extends to the press and the public at large.

"I think any potential mishap, from seating of members of Congress to the count after the fact, I know both of us have spent time with former military members, intel members, business leaders, civil society to make the case that if something happens, you have to speak up," Warner said.

Asked if he thought Republican lawmakers would speak out, the senator replied that hope springs eternal.

"I think everybody realizes what's at stake here. I mean, the irony of celebrating our 250th anniversary and this the first year we had a completely corrupt election?" Warner said. "I think people know what's at stake."

Do you have information about midterm election influence or protection efforts you would like to share? Reach out to Eric McDaniel on Signal at ericmcdaniel.92

entries.title: How Trump's attacks on voting system integrity might affect upcoming elections
entries.summary: Election law expert Rick Hasen explains Trump's interference in the midterms, including threatening local officials with criminal prosecution unless they strike alleged noncitizens from voter rolls.
entries.content:
How Trump's attacks on voting system integrity might affect upcoming elections

Election law expert Rick Hasen explains Trump's interference in the midterms, including threatening local officials with criminal prosecution unless they strike alleged noncitizens from voter rolls.

DAVE DAVIES, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Dave Davies. The midterm election is less than two weeks away. And for months, President Donald Trump has been warning that American voting systems are not to be trusted, including in his July primetime address to the nation.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Hundreds of thousands of noncitizens and dead people are listed and active on the voter rolls. And yet we still have elections with no voter ID, no proof of citizenship and tens of millions of ballots flowing aimlessly through the mail.

DAVIES: Trump has claimed that mail-in ballots may be forged, that voting machines can be hacked and that corrupt Democrats will conspire to steal votes, as he claims they did in his 2020 loss to Joe Biden. He's tried to affect the election by imposing new restrictions on registration and voting, requiring the Post Office to screen who can receive mail-in ballots and demanding that states purge thousands of people from voter rolls. Those moves have mostly been blocked by courts, but many election experts worry that Trump's claims are laying the basis to challenge the outcome of the midterms if results don't go his way.

Today, we're going to speak to two experts on elections. A little later, we'll talk to Al Schmidt, the chief elections official in the swing state of Pennsylvania. But first, we'll speak to Richard Hasen. He's director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School and founder of the popular Election Law Blog. He's author of the book "A Real Right To Vote: How A Constitutional Amendment Can Safeguard American Democracy," now in paperback, and a forthcoming book, "Unbent Arc: The Rise And Decline Of American Democracy 1964-2024." We recorded our conversation yesterday.

Well, Rick Hasen, welcome back to FRESH AIR.

RICK HASEN: It's good to be with you.

DAVIES: You know, you've written that several attempts by President Trump to interfere with the coming election have been decisively defeated. One of them was an effort mostly by the Department of Homeland Security to get states to purge large numbers of people from their voting rolls - people the administration said they had identified as likely noncitizens registered to vote. That effort, it turns out, is still active, at least in California. But first, tell us what we know about where these lists of noncitizen voters came from.

HASEN: So the United States is pretty unique compared to other advanced democracies in that we don't have a national identity card. We don't have a national database of all of our voters. We don't automatically register our voters. So we face problems here in terms of knowing who is eligible to vote and, when they move from place to place, to change their voter registration.

So the federal government has some data on citizenship. It's got something called the SAVE database. We know that this database is not all that reliable. We also know that it's not all that up to date. So sometimes it might flag someone as a noncitizen who in recent months might have been naturalized as a citizen. And so the federal government has been using the SAVE database, as well as some other commercially available databases, to try to come up with a list of citizens that they're trying to have the states compare with their own state voter registration lists to take out people who are not eligible to be voting.

DAVIES: Right. And we should note that it's been reported that the Department of Homeland Security has had hundreds of agents scouring these various state voter lists to try and find these allegedly noncitizen registered voters, right?

HASEN: Yes. So they've been doing that. One of the problems is that there are many people with the same names. And unless you have really good, identifiable information like Social Security numbers and driver's license numbers, it's possible to make mistakes. So that's one of the reasons why the federal government has sued to try to get what are called the unredacted lists that have all of that personal information.

Most states - it's against the law to provide that information to anyone. And the federal government sued 31 states and Washington D.C. And so far, they're zero for 26 in their lawsuits to try to get these unredacted voting rolls. And that's in part because our Constitution doesn't give the federal government the power to run elections. It says that states run elections. Congress can pass statutes that govern some of the aspects of congressional elections, but there's no role for the federal government. And so here you have the Trump administration trying to intrude on what's traditionally been a state and local prerogative.

DAVIES: So in some cases, the federal government - the Department of Homeland Security - has given states actual lists of people and said, look at these people. You should purge them. How have states responded to that?

HASEN: Well, Nevada is a good example. So a few months ago, the Department of Homeland Security said they had identified hundreds of thousands of noncitizens across four different states. One of them was Nevada. There were 16,000 people on this possible list. It got whittled down to 185. And eventually, when state officials investigated, it went down to zero. That is, all of the 16,000 people who were identified either were not registered to vote or were eligible to register to vote.

In California, in that same report, the Department of Homeland Security, without providing the data, said that there were up to 190,000 noncitizens. Now, in the most recent actions in California, they've whittled that number down to 20,000. And so far, they've arrested 28. And it appears from those arrests that at least some of those people either were not registered to vote or did not break the law intentionally.

DAVIES: Right. And as I understand it, this list of 20,000 names that they wanted the state of California and officials in Los Angeles to check was simply provided to them on a thumb drive with a password on a sticky note? Is that right?

HASEN: Yeah. So it's worth taking a step back and recognizing how unusual this whole set of events is. So ordinarily, there's a lot of cooperation between the federal government and state and local governments in terms of administering elections. Now we have this very different situation where the states and localities are seeing the federal government as kind of an adversary that's been threatening state and local election officials with prosecution if they don't adequately police their voting rolls in ways that the Trump administration wants.

And the idea that in the middle of an election - you know, in California, ballots are already out. We're getting into the period of in-person early voting - that in this period that the federal government would send on a thumb drive, with the password on a sticky note, the names of 20,000 possible noncitizen voters and ask 48 hours for the state to agree to go through this list and purge voters - I mean, it's just incredible. It's not the kind of thing that ever has happened that I'm aware of.

And there's a federal law called the National Voter Registration Act. It's a law that was passed when Bill Clinton was president in 1993. And it says that states can't do these last-minute voter purges because doing so risks disenfranchising eligible voters.

DAVIES: Now, as you said, 28 people were charged with either having registered or voted as noncitizens earlier this week. Some were actually arrested and taken to court. Just tell us what that experience was like, as it's been reported.

HASEN: Well, it seems clear that this was a publicity stunt that was meant to back up the federal government's attempt to get an order from a judge - a temporary restraining order that would require California to go through this list and segregate out ballots from people who are on this list. So we know that a branch of the Department of Homeland Security did a 5 a.m. raid. There were helicopters, SWAT team to arrest a man in pretty bad health. He had recently had six surgeries. He was arrested and taken into custody. And eventually, four hours later, they told him what he was charged with. He has no idea what's going on here.

What we know from what the Los Angeles Times has reported is that many of these people don't even know why they were arrested. And in the case of the man who was taken in the predawn raid, it's possible that a relative who has the same name, who is a U.S. citizen, was confused for this person who was arrested, and it may be that it is the person who is allowed to vote, whose name is on the voter list rather than the person who was arrested.

DAVIES: And I believe it was reported that the four people who on the first day made their first appearance in court often appeared in, like, shackles - right? - leg irons in some cases, and then were released on their own recognizance.

HASEN: Yes. And the federal government tipped off the New York Post, which was given an exclusive to cover this. There were photographers from the Associated Press. This was clearly an orchestrated effort to make it appear that noncitizen voting is a huge problem. The headline at the New York Post talked about a network of people conspiring to commit fraud. But there's no conspiracy charge. There's no evidence that any of the people who were charged even know each other. So this really seems to be a show, which might be for various reasons, but it doesn't seem to be for legitimate law enforcement purposes.

DAVIES: And we should note that in many states, there have been cases where voters, when they got driver's license, as many immigrants have, were registered to vote, in some cases, without their knowledge, or at least it wasn't exactly clear that they understood they were being registered, right?

HASEN: Yes. So this takes a little bit of explanation. So the 1993 law the National Voter Registration Act, among other things, provides that state offices like Departments of Motor Vehicles, have to offer opportunities for people who get their driver's license or do business at the DMV to register to vote. When you are at the DMV and you are presented with the opportunity to register to vote, you're asked if you're a citizen. And sometimes you're asked on one of those PIN pads, which I know - at least here in California, they're sometimes hard to read. It's possible that someone mischecks a box, and they inadvertently get registered to vote.

We had a situation recently in New Jersey where because of an error by a vendor of software that the Department of Motor Vehicles there used, there were 6,000 noncitizens who were inadvertently registered to vote. Those people were sent registration materials. They were sent voting materials. We know that 400 of them voted. But that doesn't necessarily prove any criminal intent. In order to be criminally liable for violating the federal law against noncitizen voting, the federal government has to prove that you willfully violated the law.

Those votes, of course, are illegal, and they need to be removed from the voting rolls. But in terms of finding a large criminal conspiracy or, you know, some kind of effort to register noncitizens and get them to vote in a particular way, we just haven't seen that. The last credible allegations of something like this go back to the 1980s in California.

DAVIES: Another effort that you note President Trump made was to get the Post Office involved in the distribution of absentee ballots. What did he do? How did that turn out?

HASEN: So President Trump has issued two executive orders on elections. So in the first executive order, he tried to get a federal agency called the United States Election Assistance Commission to change the form that the federal government has for people to register to vote to require people to provide documentary proof of citizenship, like a birth certificate or a naturalization certificate, before they can register to vote. That effort was stopped by courts, which said that the president has no role to play in the conduct of elections. That didn't deter the president. He issued a second executive order in March of this year, and among other things, it created a whole system for the United States Postal Service to become the arbiters of which mail-in ballots they would accept from states. And it was very convoluted process.

First, it required the states to provide certain ballot envelope designs, and those had to be approved by the United States Postal Service. Then each envelope had to contain a unique machine-readable barcode so that each individual envelope could be tracked to know who it's going to. And then the state would have to upload a list of their voters. And the Postal Service would have to match the envelopes that are submitted by the state with the list of voters, and it would have to reject an entire batch of these ballots if there was any discrepancy between the list and what was on the ballots.

This was a very complicated system, but what made it particularly troublesome in this election is that the Postal Service hadn't gotten its act together. It had not set up the web portal that its own rules said it was going to set up for the states to upload their citizenship to the database. And what this would have meant is that the United States Postal Service would not have been allowed to accept even a single ballot from any state because no state would be able to upload its list of citizens. It took three trips to the Supreme Court to stop the United States Postal Service from putting into effect a rule that would have shut down mail-in balloting for the 2026 elections. Now, this rule is still in litigation, and there's a chance that it will be in effect for the 2028 elections. The court orders only involve the 2026 elections. But by 2028, presumably, at least the USPS will have a working portal so that states that want to comply would be able to.

DAVIES: Richard Hasen directs the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School. We'll continue our conversation after a break. This is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR, and we're speaking with Richard Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School and founder of the Election Law Blog. Let's talk about some other efforts that might be made by the president in the course of the midterms. One thing that's been written about is that he could declare a national emergency and thereby mobilize federal resources to intervene directly in voting. What about that prospect?

HASEN: Well, the president's already declared a national emergency at the southern border. When the president declares a national emergency, it unlocks certain powers for the president. But none of those powers are involving elections. So even if Trump declares a national emergency by falsely claiming, for example, that a foreign government is trying to interfere with U.S. elections, that still doesn't give the president the power over the administration of elections. If Donald Trump declared tomorrow that we're not going to hold elections, that would have no legal effect because it's not the federal government that runs elections. It's the states and the local governments.

And Trump was on a right-wing podcast. He was asked about this. And he just said something like, stranger things have happened. So, you know, kind of keeping the conspiratorial right satisfied that he's considering this, but I think it's extremely unlikely he would do it. And if he did, I don't think it would have any effect on how our elections are actually run.

DAVIES: Another fear is that armed law enforcement personnel will appear at polling places - like, particularly ICE agents. Can that happen?

HASEN: I believe there are three different federal laws that bar armed federal officers from appearing at polling places. So it would be illegal, and if it happened, I think it would be possible to get a court order against it happening.

But I think there's a more fundamental reason why I don't think it's going to happen. Remember, we're talking about a series of congressional elections and elections for Senate as well as for state and local offices. This is not like a presidential election where there's a battleground state, like we could say it all comes down to what happens in Pennsylvania or Wisconsin. There might be a very close election for Congress in Ohio or in California. There aren't enough ICE agents to send around.

And also, we saw the reaction of the public in Minneapolis when there were these surges of ICE agents to try to engage in immigration activities. I think it would be a big risk of a political backlash against the president if there was an attempt to try to physically stop people from voting or to intimidate voters by sending ICE agents to the polls.

DAVIES: Then there's the more extreme step of seizing ballots or voting machines. And I don't - this has never happened, and I - as far as I know - in an ongoing vote, right?

HASEN: I think if the president is going to try to interfere with the elections, he's much more likely to do so on the back end of the election rather than the front end. By the front end, I mean when people are actually going and voting, millions of people going to polling places. It'd be very hard to disrupt that. It would be very public.

What I'm more worried about in the event of a very close election for control of the House or Senate is that Trump's Department of Justice might try to interfere with the tabulation process - that's the counting of ballots - or the certification process, when state officials say, yeah, here's who the official winners are. And one way that the Department of Justice could potentially get involved is by trying to get a federal court order to seize ballots or seize voting machines. The reason we care about this is because Donald Trump has said that he regrets not seizing voting machines after the 2020 election that he lost to Joe Biden and contested.

Now, we did have a seizure of ballots in 2025 in Fulton County, Georgia, that took the ballots from the 2020 election, so a long-completed election. We also had Tulsi Gabbard, the former director of national intelligence, have the Department of Homeland Security seize voting machines in Puerto Rico that were then taken and looked at by federal government workers. But what we have not had is the seizure of ballots or a voting machine in a live election - one where the winner has not yet been determined.

When ballots or machines are taken out of the possession of election officials, you break what's called the electoral chain of custody. That is, one of the ways that we know that elections are free and fair is that the ballots are always under the control of election officials, and typically with transparency measures like cameras or other ways of observing, to make sure that no one is meddling with the ballots. If ballots are taken out of the custody of election officials, ballots could be added to or altered or taken away. It would be incredibly dangerous. It would require getting a search warrant from a federal judge.

And so one of the things that we've been doing at the Safeguarding Democracy Project, and others have been working on, is trying to educate judges. Judges know a lot about criminal law. They know a lot about search warrants. They don't know a lot about how elections are run. And so we're trying to explain the kind of irreparable harm that can happen if ballots are allowed to be taken outside the custody of election officials. There are ways to satisfy legitimate law enforcement purposes if there is, in fact, probable cause that a crime has been committed. There are ways to protect those ballots as evidence without breaking the electoral chain of custody.

DAVIES: We're going to take another break here. Let me reintroduce you. Richard Hasen is director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School and founder of the Election Law Blog. He'll be back after this short break. I'm Dave Davies, and this is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF BILL FRISELL'S "WASHINGTON POST MARCH")

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR. I'm Dave Davies. And we're talking about the potential effect of President Trump's repeated warnings of fraud in the midterm election, less than two weeks away. While Trump's attempts to impose restrictions on registration and voting have largely failed in the courts, some election experts worry that his claims are designed to lay the basis for challenging the outcome of the November 3 voting if things don't go his way. We're speaking with Richard Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School and founder of the popular Election Law Blog.

The other prospect that people are talking about is that after the election, that the clerk of the United States House of Representatives, who was appointed by the speaker, Mike Johnson, could refuse to seat Democrats in closely contested races. What's the check on that?

HASEN: Well - so to begin with, there's a political check. If, for example, the news organizations have said that Democrats have won enough elections to retake control of Congress - if the clerk, who is a bureaucrat, came in and said, well, no. These races are contested. We're not going to let these people be seated and get to vote for speaker of the House - I think that would be politically very dangerous. That would look like a literal coup d'etat. That is, it would be trying to turn an election loser into an election winner, in this case, through fraud.

If it did happen, which I think is very unlikely, I think there would be resort to the courts. And courts would come in. Now, ordinarily, a court wouldn't interfere with a congressional process. The - under the separation of powers, that would be a political question. But the clerk who works for the House is not the House. And so I think the courts could hear such a challenge. And it's extremely unlikely that, both politically and legally, this kind of move could happen if, in fact, the Democrats have easily taken control of the House.

Now, that leads me to a more general point about what we expect after November 3. It's all about the margins. If, in fact, we do not have a close election for control of the House or the Senate, I would be very surprised to see any attempts to try to wholesale change the results of the elections so that control of the House or Senate could flip.

If the elections are very close - for example, suppose that control of the Senate comes down to who wins in Alaska - Alaska, which takes a very long time to count their ballots because of their rural populations and where they use ranked-choice voting, which takes longer to tabulate results. If it comes down to one seat, then I think all bets are off. And then I'm very concerned that the Trump administration will try to do things to manipulate the outcome of the elections.

DAVIES: I know you've written about campaign finance. And the spending in this election is truly unprecedented by individuals. We've seen reporting that Elon Musk has pumped 276 million into the midterms, a figure that's probably out of date by now. Over 150 million has gone through a couple of transactions into the Texas state Senate race. What's this doing to our democracy? And what can we do about it?

HASEN: So there's been a real sea change since the United States Supreme Court decided the Citizens United case in 2010. Some of it is legal change - the creation of super PACs. But even the seeds for super PACs, which are independent groups that can raise unlimited sums from individuals, corporations and unions - even the seeds for that were planted in a 1976 case called Buckley v. Valeo. But something has changed psychologically on the part of big donors in that they're no longer shy about putting their money into elections.

And so just to give you some statistics, the first donor who gave at least $100 million to groups in a federal election was Sheldon Adelson back in 2018. We only had one or two people or couples in this category. A hundred million dollars - just an obscene amount of money for one person to be able to give an election.

By the 2024 elections, we had nine individuals and couples who fit into that category. And Elon Musk set the record with almost $300 million in spending. I think he's likely to exceed that in a midterm election, which is even more astounding, when typically the spending is much lower than in a presidential election year. It's a fundamentally unfair system in which we allow the wealthiest of Americans to have outsized influence not only over who's elected by increasing the chances that the candidate they support will be elected thanks to all of the campaign dollars, but also outsized influence over what elected officials are going to do once they're in office.

So if you are the recipient of Elon Musk's generosity, you're going to be very solicitous of his interests and what he wants to do. And if you're on the other side, you might fear doing something that might antagonize Elon Musk for fear that he could unleash really astronomical sums against you. And so the system - we might call it corruption. It certainly is an unequal system where the wealthiest among us are able to translate their economic power into political power.

DAVIES: And what's the prospect for doing something about it?

HASEN: The prospects for doing something about it in the short term are quite low because the current regime we have is the product of Supreme Court decisions, especially over the last 20 years. We have a very conservative Supreme Court that, on campaign finance issues, takes a very libertarian view of the First Amendment and sees most limits on money and politics as unconstitutional - as a violation of the rights of free speech and association.

So how could you change that? You either have to change the Constitution or you have to change the Supreme Court. Both of those things are very difficult to do. Actually, I think it would be probably easier to change the Supreme Court than to get through a constitutional amendment, which requires supermajorities in both the House and Senate and supermajority of states to approve a constitutional amendment.

So I think there's going to be a lot of pressure if Democrats retake the House and the Senate and the presidency in 2029 to try to deal with some of the issues related to our democracy, from campaign finance to partisan gerrymandering to the Supreme Court's evisceration of the Voting Rights Act.

DAVIES: Well, briefly returning to the election in front of us, you know, The Washington Post recently reported that a group of former national security officials are warning state election officials to be on the lookout for meddling and interference on November 3. I'm wondering what you're going to be doing that day and how you anticipate affecting this - following it, covering it.

HASEN: Usually Election Day is pretty quiet for me because things generally go smoothly. Of course, there's going to be someplace where there's a power outage and machines are not working, or a county didn't provide enough ballots to a polling place. There might be some last-minute skirmishing about whether polls need to be kept open an extra hour or two for people who were not able to vote. But it should be quiet on Election Day, especially because I think many people have been heeding the advice of election experts to vote early if you can. And I would say, if you're going to vote by mail, vote as early as possible or put that ballot in a dropbox or bring it to a voting center if that's allowed in your state. So hopefully it will be quiet.

It'll be the day after Election Day or a couple of days after Election Day when we'll really have a sense of whether or not we're going to make it through this period. And in 2020, I warned that we would have a real danger of an attempt to interfere with free and fair elections - a peaceful transition of power. And people said that I was too alarmist. This time around, as I see the bulwarks of our democracy - the states, the courts and the people - protecting free and fair elections, I'm more optimistic. And people are saying I'm too optimistic. So let's hope that it goes that way.

DAVIES: Well, Rick Hasen, thank you so much for speaking with us again.

HASEN: It was great to be with you.

DAVIES: Richard Hasen is director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the UCLA Law School. Since we recorded our conversation, there was another large political contribution. Michael Bloomberg gave $80 million to the Democrats. Coming up, we hear from Al Schmidt, chief election official in the swing state of Pennsylvania. This is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF WES MONTGOMERY'S "4 ON 6")

entries.title: Why local officials are feeling 'on edge' as election day approaches
entries.summary: Al Schmidt is the chief election official in the state of Pennsylvania. President Trump's insults put him in danger during the 2020 ballot count. Now Schmidt talks about preparing for the midterms.
entries.content:
Why local officials are feeling 'on edge' as election day approaches

Al Schmidt is the chief election official in the state of Pennsylvania. President Trump's insults put him in danger during the 2020 ballot count. Now Schmidt talks about preparing for the midterms.

DAVE DAVIES, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. Our next guest, Al Schmidt, had a memorable experience in the 2020 presidential election, which Donald Trump has long claimed was stolen. Back then, Schmidt was the lone Republican on the three-member election board of Philadelphia, a Democratic stronghold in the key swing state of Pennsylvania. Schmidt helped supervise and publicly defended the integrity of the long and tedious count of hundreds of thousands of mail-in ballots. The count took days and eventually gave Democrat Joe Biden the state's 20 electoral votes. But it earned Schmidt nationally reported insults from then-President Trump and threats from some of his followers.

Today Schmidt is secretary of the commonwealth, the chief voting official for all of Pennsylvania, which will again be a critically contested state in a national election with high stakes for Donald Trump. There are four competitive congressional races in Pennsylvania, which could help decide control of the House of Representatives. We thought it would be useful to get Schmidt's take on this election season and what he expects and fears from the voting on November 3 and the count and certification to follow.

Before we begin, I should note that Al Schmidt and I have known each other for a long time. I was a political reporter for many years for the Philadelphia Daily News and public radio when Al was active in local Republican politics.

Al Schmidt, welcome to FRESH AIR.

AL SCHMIDT: Great to be back with you, Dave.

DAVIES: Let's spend a moment on that harrowing experience following the 2020 election. And to remind listeners, this was the first COVID election - right? - 2020, when mail ballots, normally not common in the United States, were all over the country. Back then, Philadelphia was typically used to processing about 13,000, 14,000...

SCHMIDT: That's right.

DAVIES: ...Absentee ballots. Now there were over 370,000 mail ballots. And the state election code prevented your election workers from even opening the envelopes until Election Day, which meant it was going to take a long time. It was expected that Donald Trump would be ahead on the machine vote because he had discouraged people from using mail ballots. Tell us what it was like to try and get all those ballots counted as quickly as you could.

SCHMIDT: Yes. And to help sort of set the scene here, you're right. It was the first election that Pennsylvania had with no-excuse mail-ballot voting, meaning any voter could vote by mail. Philadelphia also had essentially new voting systems in-person at the polls that election. We also had the COVID environment possibly at its peak, and we also had civil unrest in Philadelphia. So we were trying to manage our way through all of those different challenges.

With mail-ballot voting, we had about half of our voters, probably because of the COVID environment at the time, vote by mail. That's a lot in a presidential election with predictably very high turnout. But one thing that puts Pennsylvania at a disadvantage then and now is that our counties can't begin processing mail ballots until 7 a.m. on election morning. Other states begin that process days, if not weeks, in advance.

DAVIES: They can rip open the envelopes so that you're ready to process the ballots, right?

SCHMIDT: That's right. So on election night at 8 p.m., they're ready to report the results of what they had worked on for many days, if not weeks. In Pennsylvania, that's not the case. So in 2020, obviously, we had the in-person results coming in first - those are people who voted at the polls on Election Day - followed by these waves of updates for voting by mail as they were tabulated by our counties.

DAVIES: Right. So you would give regular updates on what the count of the mail ballot showed. And what was happening was you could see that Donald Trump's lead in the state was shrinking as more Democratic votes rather than Republican were reflected in the mail ballots. It got to a point where it got ugly and personal, didn't it? I mean, threats, right?

SCHMIDT: Yes. So we had had fairly general threats prior to that, like, you're going to get what's coming to you, or things that, you know, don't really rise to a level of concern for me, especially at this point. But as it went on, they certainly got a lot more specific, naming my children, providing my address in the threats, obviously graphic descriptions of the violence.

So I really relied on law enforcement - especially the Philadelphia Police Department, which did an incredible job and I'm always going to be grateful - for really taking care of my family. Like, we were inside the convention center. We had many, many police officers and sheriffs present outside. That's probably why threats were targeting your family, right? You're not there. It's all about trying to keep you from doing your job. So we couldn't allow ourselves to be distracted from doing our job because of the threats targeting our families.

DAVIES: Was your family relocated?

SCHMIDT: My family was relocated. And then we had around-the-clock police protection for many months after that because the threats continued, certainly leading up to the certification of the presidential election many weeks later. So when I walked the dog, police were coming with us. When we took the kids sledding, the police were there. It was just a constant presence.

DAVIES: Yeah. Yeah.

SCHMIDT: Thanksgiving, Christmas.

DAVIES: I don't...

SCHMIDT: And so...

DAVIES: ...Want to be - yeah.

SCHMIDT: ...Sort of surreal. I don't mean to laugh about it, but it was a surreal environment. And we got to, you know, know them pretty well. And I - like I said, I'm grateful.

DAVIES: So you're still a registered Republican. And...

SCHMIDT: I am.

DAVIES: You're serving a Democratic governor in a swing state. So here we are. And President Trump has been very, very active in warning that there will be fraud and that mail ballots are subject to fraud. And not just talking. I mean, he's tried to do things and get the government to do things which would affect the voting in this election. Give us a sense of the kind of incoming demands you have gotten from the federal government.

SCHMIDT: Well, there have been several, primarily from the Department of Justice and from the Department of Homeland Security. The biggest, of course, was a demand that we provide Pennsylvania's voter rolls to DOJ. And not just the publicly available voter rolls but the Social Security numbers of every registered voter in Pennsylvania that we have, every driver's license number and all the rest. So that's information that we are, obviously, typically prohibited from sharing. It would not be legal for us to share. And it was clear that we weren't going to provide that information, and we declined their demand.

That information has to be safeguarded. Nothing would jeopardize election integrity more than Social Security numbers and driver's license numbers being shared with multiple government agencies with unclear control over that sort of information. So we declined. The courts ruled in our favor, as they did in more than two dozen others at this point in these lawsuits against DOJ.

DAVIES: Right. I believe also, the Department of Justice told you that there were 14,000 noncitizens registered to vote in Pennsylvania. Do I have this right?

SCHMIDT: Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security. The accusation was that we have north of 14,000 noncitizens registered to vote in Pennsylvania because of whatever data matching, using whatever datasets in whatever way that led them to reach that conclusion.

DAVIES: This came your way when? Like, two months ago? Or...

SCHMIDT: Some months ago.

DAVIES: OK.

SCHMIDT: And then we responded - rightly, I think - asking for more information on this. Like, what data was used? From what datasets? How did the matching occur? What do you consider a match and not a match? Like, I have the same name as my dad. Would we show up as a match, as the same person? Because they obviously did not have Social Security number or driver's license number, which is a unique identifier that everybody has, that would be necessary to do that sort of matching. And even when that matches, you still have to do the hard work. You still have to do the research.

And I was a Republican election commissioner in Philadelphia for 10 years. Election integrity is very important, from my point of view. And it's important to handle it responsibly and not just cry wolf every time you have some sort of data match based on garbage information.

DAVIES: And so you responded, saying, give us more information. And then what happened?

SCHMIDT: We had a virtual meeting with them where we asked more questions. The answers to those questions obviously were insufficient to provide us with any sense of security or certainty related to the reliability of their data. And that was the end of it, other than a letter from the Department of Justice saying, as you currently know, you are under criminal investigation.

DAVIES: Criminal investigation?

SCHMIDT: Yes.

DAVIES: When you're under criminal investigation, you generally know that by other means, like you get a grand jury subpoena or investigators come to you to talk to you? That...

SCHMIDT: You would. And it also doesn't usually start - as you must know, or as you know. But there's nothing certainly special about that. Every secretary who refused DOJ's demand received the same letter.

DAVIES: We'll take a break here. Let me reintroduce you. We are speaking with Al Schmidt. He is Pennsylvania's secretary of the commonwealth, the state's chief election official. We'll talk more after this short break. This is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF ROBBEN FORD & BILL EVANS' "PIXIES")

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR. And as we anticipate potential controversies involving the midterm election in two weeks, we're speaking with election integrity experts and an official involved in supervising elections. Our guest in this segment is Al Schmidt. He is Pennsylvania's secretary of the Commonwealth, the state's chief election official. Pennsylvania, a perennial battleground state, has four competitive congressional elections this year.

As you look forward to the election, just a little less than two weeks away, what worries you?

SCHMIDT: Well, anyone involved with an election administration worries about everything all the time. And any issue, big or small, can be exploited to undermine confidence in election results. So that's always a concern. It's never a question of things not being a concern. But obviously, now we've had to consider a lot more things than we did in the past, such as the threat of federal interference or anything like that. So we work with our counties. We do tabletop exercises with them. We work with our state partners - Pennsylvania State Police and National Guard and others - to work through different scenarios so that, should anything occur from any direction, we're all prepared and can communicate and know what everybody's roles and responsibilities are.

DAVIES: There's a lot of discussion about how common or uncommon election fraud is in the country. And you're in a better position than most people to have an opinion about this because you participated in elections not just as an election official, but as a Republican candidate running for office in a city run by Democrats. You also, when you were a city commissioner on the election board in Philadelphia, did a study of election improprieties and fraud. So what did you find? I mean, is there fraud out there?

SCHMIDT: Well, we did find evidence of cases of voter fraud, as we always have in Pennsylvania and elsewhere. It's just that it occurs extremely infrequently and has never had any impact on the outcome of an election. But that's not to shrug it off. And I made several referrals to the U.S. attorney's office and to the district attorney's office and attorney general's office and worked with all three levels of law enforcement in Pennsylvania and in Philadelphia to investigate and, when warranted, prosecute and hold people accountable who did commit acts of voter fraud. And it was always at a very local level, affecting very small races because that's where a handful of votes can really impact the outcome of an election, not necessarily President the United States or any statewide race.

DAVIES: One of the things you hear about corruption in Philadelphia is that dead people vote. You actually looked into this once, right? Tell us that story.

SCHMIDT: I did at great length. It is the easiest thing in the world to prove if it occurred. You know when a vote was cast, and you know when a voter died. You have a record of when the person died, and you have a record of when their vote was cast. So we worked comparing the Social Security Death Index against the voter rolls and narrowed it down to, in the end, it was about 10 to 12 cases that I was sure that we got. I was sure that we had identified 10 to 12 cases where a dead voter had voted. But you can't just rely on a data match and say that's evidence of anything. It was only a lead. So that's where you had to do the hard work. You had to knock on doors.

The first door I knocked on in North Philly, I remember the woman answered the door, and her record was that she was deceased. It's just that she had the same name as someone else in the same precinct or division in Philadelphia, and her record was canceled, not the person with the same name. So it showed up as a false positive. There was that, there was where people would go to vote, and someone else in the same place, usually mother and daughter or father and son, with the same name, and they would sign in the other person's spot, not in their spot. So it was never a question of more votes being cast...

DAVIES: The voter roll book that the election worker would say, sign here.

SCHMIDT: That's right. So it would be Al Schmidt followed by Al Schmidt, and they would sign where it had the one person, not the other. It wasn't a fraudulent vote or anything else like that. It was signing the poll book under the wrong person's name with the same name. And in the end, we ended up with zero out of that 10 to 12. It was kind of disappointing 'cause I thought for sure that, you know, you heard so much about all this over all these years, and you put in all that hard work. And, I mean, it was a relief knowing that you didn't have voter fraud going on. There was certainly something important to take from it all. But, you know, you end up in this search, and in the end, everything that could be done was done, and there was no evidence of it.

DAVIES: I'm wondering if the experience of 2020 has affected people's willingness to serve on election boards and assist in elections.

SCHMIDT: We track it at Department of State, and we've certainly seen an increase in turnover when it comes to the people responsible for elections, and there are many reasons for it, right? Sometimes people are just ready to retire. For others, it's because of the environment, the way that it's been around elections and also the requirements to be an election director have changed so much since I got involved in 2011 and 2012. So you have to be a lot more public facing. You have to be better at communicating. We have never had so much interest in elections. People have a lot of questions. It's just incumbent upon us to provide them with truthful answers to their questions so that they're not deceived by people who lie for a living.

DAVIES: Al Schmidt, I wish you a smooth and peaceful Election Day. Thank you for coming in and speaking with us.

SCHMIDT: Thank you, Dave.

DAVIES: Al Schmidt is Pennsylvania's Secretary of the Commonwealth, the state's chief election official.

(SOUNDBITE OF PSYCHOGRASS' "HIGH HAM")

DAVIES: On Tomorrow's show - actor Betty Gilpin, if you watched the series "Widow's Bay," you saw her Emmy-winning performance as a woman in the 1700s who realizes her new husband may be at the center of a Satanic curse. She now stars with Ethan Hawke in the new season of the FX show "The Lowdown." She also starred as Mary Todd Lincoln in the Broadway play "Oh, Mary!" I hope you can join us.

To keep up with what's on the show and get highlights of our interviews, follow us on Instagram - @nprfreshair. FRESH AIR's executive producer is Sam Briger. Our technical director at engineer is Audrey Bentham. Our interviews and reviews are produced and edited by Phyllis Myers, Ann Marie Baldonado, Lauren Krenzel, Therese Madden, Monique Nazareth, Thea Chaloner, Susan Nyakundi, Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez-Wisler.
